utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms Residovic, you are still cross-examining. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back now to what we were talking about yesterday. Mr Gligorevic, when I asked you yesterday, you responded that in Celebici you were questioned by just one person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was questioned by just one person.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in your statement given to the Prosecutor last year you stated that there were three persons. One was a Croat and there were two Muslims. Taking into account the passage of time, can you tell me that you remember now clearly that there were three persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe there was a misunderstanding. I was personally interrogated but by one judge. I don't know whether he was a judge actually. The others were questioned by another judge at another place, but in front of the same building. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also stated that you signed in Cyrillic and that they provided both the questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr Gligorevic, that they wrote down what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what it was that they wrote down? Did they write that you had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and also that I was -- used it to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although it was not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You signed a statement in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That judge forced me to do so. He said: "Yes, you are a teacher. You should know Cyrillic script. Please sign in Cyrillic".

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the Trial Chamber is not familiar with our alphabets. Can you please now sign on this paper in Cyrillic and in the Roman alphabet. Can I please ask the usher to provide assistance? Thank you, your Honours. The only reason for this is I want to tell you in Bosnia-Herzegovina both scripts were in use, both the Cyrillic and the Roman script. Since the witness spoke about the manner in which he signed his statement, I think that I will need the signature in the course of my cross-examination. Thank you very much and thank you, Mr Gligorevic. This statement, was it typed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was written down by hand by one of the interrogators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, you did that because you thought that if you did not sign, you would endanger your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So did they read the statement out to you later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The judge read out the statement and he said -- he told me to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So when he read the statement to you, you remember that he wrote down that you had weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had to put that there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what weapon you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think that he wrote down that it was a rifle, I think M-48.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he mention any rounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also said ...

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he -- was it written down who issued the rifle to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Branislav Gligorevic, nicknamed Beko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the statement contain that you were issued the rifle from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it written in the statement that you took part in keeping watches or sentries in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it written there that the night before your arrest you were on a position in the wood called Gaj further up from the village of Upper Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for sure where, although it was written down, but I can't recall that now. I can't recall anything about the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you remember some details because this man read out the statement to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He read it out. Whether it was actually what was written there I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the questioning and the signing of the statement you were not abused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, but I was threatened.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, if the facts that you were talking about now were true, can we then agree that these facts during a state of war would be significant for a person who was questioning you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know the reason for.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If other Serbs from Bradina were to confirm you did have all those things that were written down in the statement, do you claim they are not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I object to this question, your Honour. It is trying to make him say things that has no foundation in the investigation or anywhere else. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, you heard the objection of the prosecutor. My Defendant is charged with particular offences, amongst other things the allegations that are the subject of my cross-examination. He is charged as a direct perpetrator, not only as having command responsibility. I think I have the right during cross-examination to ask pertinent questions of the witness. Will you allow me, your Honours, to continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I am afraid the witness has started by denying the statement which was credited to him, and he has stated it was made under threats, which strictly speaking is inadmissible. I do not see how you can continue on that line. Statements which are obtained by threats or duress are inadmissible. It is on the basis of that statement you are making this cross-examination. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, I think I may be wrong and thank you for your caution, but I can investigate the truth of what this witness is talking about. I appreciate your remarks and I do not think that I will continue questioning in this vein. He confirmed that he had been questioned and in which manner and I will now move on to my other questions, but I would like you to allow me to ask this witness the questions about that, because these have to do with the allegations against my client. Thank you very much. Mr Gligorevic, you stated that you had come to Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: do you know that the JNA from Hadzici supplied in secret the weapons to Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that two shipments of weapons came to Zara Mrkajic in Bradina. These were fifty rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are Hadzici adjacent -- municipality adjacent to the Konjic municipality and they attach in the part of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified before the Trial Chamber that you were a teacher both in Bradina and in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We know that, but can you confirm that at that age the children are being taught the geography of their area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, can I then show you this map and ask you to recognise or to point out the places that I am talking about? Can this map be given to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will the usher kindly assist in taking it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please put it on the ELMO so we can see what is shown to the witness. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. Thank you, Mr Ostberg. I just wanted to suggest that. Mr Gligorevic, would you be so kind as to point on this map where Sarajevo is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then locate Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please point to the main route from Sarajevo to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you now point to Bradina, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, can you now point to where Hadzici is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Somewhere around here, I think, between Sarajevo and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to put a mark with a pen on that place and write down Hadzici as you think they are located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around here, I think more or less. I couldn't point it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you just to put it. Nobody is going to check on our ability to produce maps, but this is approximately where Hadzici is. Mr Gligorevic, can you please tell me where is Pozaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pozaric is, roughly speaking, between Hadzici and Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the spot where Pozaric is located? I would also like you to point to the place called Tarcin. Thank you very much, Mr Gligorevic. I would like to ask you now: Tarcin and Pozaric are local communes that belong to the municipality of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask, since the witness has written down the maps, I would like to tender this as Defence Exhibit D1/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I ask: to prove what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But this is a defence exhibit, because I believe she is trying to get at, that the services were supplying arms to Bradina. These were the places. This was of course on the main route to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It can be understood in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: She is merely laying the background for the next evidence. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you very much, your Honours. As a teacher in Hadzici, you knew that Hadzici was a strong centre of the former JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not spend a very long time in Hadzici. I was there shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that they had plant and factories for maintenance there, maintenance both of cars, vehicles and probably also weapons. Also military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the fact that you had come to Bradina from such a place the basis for the way you were treated as a detainee in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody has told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating commission in Celebici did not tell you that? Do you think they could have suspected that there was some kind of connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr Gligorevic. Since you do not have that kind of knowledge, I would like to repeat this group of questions and please can you verify that I understood you correctly. You gave a statement in Celebici outside of the command building, squatting down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You gave it to one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The statement was written down by hand by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The statement was read out to you by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He read it out, but whether it was actually written down, what he read, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You signed a statement in Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the only questioning that you were subjected to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Gligorevic. I will now go on to a different kind of questioning. You confirmed before this court that in early October you were transferred from Celebici to Musala prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on October 4th.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At Musala you probably heard of the tragic case when the sports hall was shelled, when a dozen prisoners died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, but I was not there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But while you were there, did you hear that even before that and after that shells fell close to Musala every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they fell near and far.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It also happened when you were at Musala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, as regards your exchange, the investigation against you and the proceedings conducted and for which you claimed that the proceedings were not conducted at all, I would like to ask you several more questions. Do you know that a certain number of Serbs from Bradina were convicted by the Mostar District Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how many of them. What I know, there were two people from Bradina in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was Branislav Mrkajic. He was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. This sentence, he served it, but he was not released up until he was exchanged. The second one was Dravko Djordjic from Ludici.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you a document, and I would like to ask you to confirm what the document is, if you can. I apologise, your Honours. I left the document there at my desk. I would like to ask for this document, together with the translation, to be submitted both to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecutor and to all the defence counsel: this is for Mr Gligorevic: Mr Gligorevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the questioning, the first thing that strikes me is the date is 14th January 1992/3. I do not know what is the correct -- what would be the correct date of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 14th January 1993. 2 has been corrected to 3. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Can I continue, your Honours? I would like to ask for the signature given by Mr Gligorevic to be placed under the ELMO. Mr Gligorevic, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks like my signature, but I do not remember this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which one is your signature? There are about five persons who have signed it. Which one is his signature? Number 2, number 3, number 4, number 5, which one? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I think that Mr Gligorevic should tell us which his signature is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my first and last name are where it is written: "Statement given by". But I think this is falsified, this is forgery. I can't remember that, can't remember the statement at all.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This record, is this the record from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which one resembles your signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which one resembles your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one on the right-hand side, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the statement was made by hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This record was typed. Mr Gligorevic, you said you were questioned by one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And here you were questioned by five people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what we have here. This kind of interrogation -- this interrogation never existed, this can only be falsified. I think if you have to undergo such a thing, you can't forget it, and I do not remember anything apart from what I've told you about in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this has to do with the questioning at Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what is written, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 1 there is the signature of the interrogator. Can you recognise the last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably ... no.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I help you maybe? Do you recognise the name of Jasminka Dzumhur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that person very well. In the times of the former Yugoslavia we used to work together for the municipality. She was a very high official in the municipality and I was some kind of a representative in the local commune of Bradina, so we used to meet quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, your signature on this statement was not done in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but whoever wanted to sign with my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you -- does the name of Pozdar Ismeta mean anything to you? It is right there in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know her personally, but I think she was at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, do you know that in December 1992 a commission was established and its task was to interrogate all the detainees in Celebici once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that. What I know is that some people later on were taken to court, that court was in the same place where it used to be previously, at the junction in the centre of the town, but just very few people, just a couple of people. Two or three went to Buturovic Polje. There was also some kind of a court there. That was also just a few people.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just once more: you confirmed that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I said it looked like my signature, but I do not remember signing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not refer to the contents of the text. I just refer to your signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It resembled my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I suggest that since the witness assumes that this could be his signature that this document also be tendered as the next Defence Exhibit. One more thing, your Honours. I told you yesterday that I received some documents from the Konjic court, where the court questioned persons -- the persons signed here under number 1 and they determined there was a mistake in the date. They claimed that the statement was given on 14th January 1993. Yesterday we had these documents translated and I would like to tender, together with the other documents that I will present to the witness, that these documents be tendered as defence exhibits. Is it accepted as D 1/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object to putting in these documents. The witness has said that it resembles his signature, but he can't confirm that he ever signed it. He says he can't recognise it. He says that he has never been through interrogation like this. There are some difficulties with the dates and we do not know how these are produced. I think this calls for some investigation and I cannot see any possibility to bring in a document with questions like this one. He has not recognised it and not authenticated it. So I object to it being admitted as evidence in this case. Thank you, your Honours. I think I will come back to this question any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you produce some witness who can prove this document later? Will you produce some witness who will say he signed it in his presence? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then we can mark it at this stage for the purpose of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course, your Honour. If a witness can be produced who says he took this statement and he signed it in his presence, then of course I have no objection, but for the time being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let it be marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- it could not be. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Listen. During cross-examination this witness stated clearly -- there are authorities that when a witness says something by threats or duress that document could not be admissible. It is not admissible in the way in which you dealt with it. He signed it after threats. He said he was not familiar with those things that were written. They just read them to him. So he could not in those circumstances claim them. I do not see how you can identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just for clarification, if I might, I believe the court is confused because there are two statements. The first one at Celebici Miss Residovic is not trying to get marked because that is the one he stated he made under duress. This one he never made under duress. For clarification purposes this is the statement given at Musala not at Celebici, so you know there are two statements we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I am not confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not confused at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: It is clear there are two statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Maybe I was confused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you will produce evidence that this document was signed voluntarily by him, so for the purpose of not exhibiting it, we can mark it so we know which document we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, he could not even, except he is identifying it himself. If he identifies it you can then tender it for identification and it might not be admitted until it is proved, not before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are not exhibiting it. We are just marking it for purposes of identification. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, can this document be marked and then accepted as Defence Exhibit at the time when the defence provides valid evidence that this is a valid document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think it is safer for you even at that stage to prove it through who you think can prove it? It is easier. If somebody can vouch these things were done in his presence, you tender it to him. He will give his statements and it will be admissible as such. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I have here with me the last page of the statement given by this witness to the prosecutor last year. This part of the statement is signed with the signature that is completely identical. Can the Trial Chamber have a look at that signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If you are trying to prove his signature, you can prove it whichever way you can. If you have an identical signature, you put it to him and then know how to go about it. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Can the witness have a look at this undisputed signature from the statement given to the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can do so. Show it to him. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Now we have three signatures: the undisputed signature on the statement given to the prosecutor; the signature made before this court; and the signature on the document. I would like that all three signatures be placed on the ELMO, just so that the witness could identify his own signature. Can you now show the second signature that you signed here? Is this your signature? This signature here, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now show the signature that you signed now before this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the upper one. This is your signature in Roman script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the signature on the document dated 14th January 1993. Can you now confirm that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't. I am telling you I can't recall. I don't think that interrogation ever took place, and I think you can always forge a signature. By the way, I would like to know if you know the members sitting on this committee. Apart from Jasminka Dzumhur, who were the members who were on the committee?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We would like the Trial Chamber to mark for identification purposes the document where the witness recognised his signature and the document on which the witness placed his signature today and the last page of his statement given to the prosecutor, where he identified his signature as undisputedly his?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually trying to show the identity between the signatures, among the three signatures, that they are identical, that is what you are trying to show.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and I would like to ask for these two undisputed signatures be marked for identification purposes as defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know what it is for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I object even to that. If the first document cannot be admitted, if it is not authenticated, what good do the other two do? He can just accept "I wrote these two signatures" but the third one cannot be compared with it because it is not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Or she wants them exhibited so later on they can be compared. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Just for identification purposes. I do not intend to use them in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: All you want to show is that the signatures are identical. That is possible. I see nothing wrong in that, but if, apart from that, you want to go further, merely because they are identical that ... problems might arise. Only for identification of the signatures, then that is acceptable. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you very much. Just for identification purposes. Can you now please present to the witness the following document for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to see a translation and a copy of this before it is put to the witness, and the court also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Would you be so kind as to distribute the translation of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We need the original also, please. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The original is on the ELMO. Mr Gligorevic, is this document written by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this document in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, you gave this document a year after your arrival to Celebici. That was in June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the date here. Probably it happened like that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this document you wrote that you had been abused on the occasion of your arrest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read this. Could I please read it first in order to see whether that is what is written?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that all your property was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also wrote down in your own hand what kind of weapons you had and who you received it from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what is written, although one needs to write that down so as not to have a different statement from the one at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr Gligorevic, you recognised -- you identified this statement as having been written in your hand and signed in your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the answer? What was the answer? Please go a little slower. We have not got his answer yet. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): You identified this statement as having been written in your hand and as a statement that you signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the Trial Chamber to accept this document as Defence Exhibit D1/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I take a position to object or not object, I would like to know if this document was signed under some kind of threat or duress or the circumstances are absolutely unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has not said so. He did not say it was. If it was, he would have said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: To me there was some -- about the gun there were some comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, you did not suggest it to him. He did not say so. If there was duress in signing it or making the statement which he made in his own hand, he would have said so. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Is this accepted as a Defence Exhibit, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. He said he made this statement. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr Gligorevic, you wanted to know who the members of the commission who interrogated you on 14th January 1993 were. Would you please show to Mr Gligorevic this document? I would also like to ask you to present the Trial Chamber with the translation of the said document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We are referring here to the one dated June 6th, 1993? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): No, your Honours. This is the document dated 14th January and the witness asked if I could show him the members of the commission who signed the document also. So if I can now show both to you and to the witness the members of the commission so that the witness may perhaps identify them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry but --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, do you know any of the members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, apart from Jasminka Dzumhur, who I mentioned, who I knew before the war. I also saw her once at Musala, when she came there, but I do not know the others.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, on this list of the commission you recognise the name of Jasminka Dzumhur; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She is the only person I know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I for the same reasons as the way to identify one of the members of the commission of the 14th January also submit this document to the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I object, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Only because he identified one of them out of five, out of that group, he could not have done that. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, your Honours. This one person signed under number 1 on the statement disputed by the witness. It is possible that this person may appear before this Tribunal as a witness. Since he recognised this person and identified her as a person he knows, that is the reason why I would like this document to be marked for identification purposes, tendered for the purposes of identification of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not that person who is tendering it. You are tendering it through someone else, who is objecting to the rest of it, and he did not say at any stage all the five of them were acting together with respect to him. He never said so. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. The defence will then try to identify this document and to determine its importance in some other manner more suited to this Tribunal. May I now show to the witness another document and, of course, to submit to you the translation of the document? Mr Gligorevic, is the date of your arrest stated in this document, the date of your capture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a document I see for the first time in my life. It could have been printed out a couple of days ago. Nobody has ever given or shown anything like this to me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document states that a rifle and bullets were taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tell you this is the first time ever I see something of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be presented to the court in some other appropriate manner. Mr Gligorevic, do you know what amnesty is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only assume, but can you help me out?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you this is the decision of the competent authority which can then amnesty a person from any proceedings, is that what you would think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when a very high state organ, yes, gives mercy to someone.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, have you ever received amnesty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, not. I spent a lot of time in the camp in the first to the last day the camp lasted. After me the camp at Musala remained empty.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask for this document to be presented to Mr Gligorevic and to you, your Honours. This has to do with the proceedings conducted against Mr Gligorevic. Mr Gligorevic, did you receive this document at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. This is also something I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how you came to be on the exchange list if such proceedings were conducted against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. The negotiators are the ones who know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in Bosnia-Herzegovina now no proceedings are conducted against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I do not live there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that you can freely go to your village if you want to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very good, but that village does not exist any more.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The town of Konjic still exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But my village, Bradina, I think is today still a desert.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As many others, and we are here to build new ones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately I do not know why we had to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Gligorevic. Your Honours, I have some more questions. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr Gligorevic, in your statement given to the Prosecutor and in your testimony before this court you said that in Bradina and in other parts of the Republic there were village centres set up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were village centres.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what did they keep watch over, these village centres? Houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I did not take part in that, and I spent there a very short time, but I assume they were guarding their own village.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If they guard their own village and there is a road going through a village, it is logical.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Railway lines, if the railway line goes through the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me. The main route goes through Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the only railway line linking Sarajevo and central and northern Bosnia with the sea also goes there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, if these sentries were guarding this road and the railway line, it would be impossible to go from Sarajevo to Konjic on a normal route; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether one could go through there or not. I spent only a very short time there. I also know, which I explained to your colleague last time round, that these roads were blocked. There was a tunnel near Konjic which was destroyed, and also in the direction of Sarajevo it was all blocked with parts of excavators, with sand and logs.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Gligorevic, but you also explained to my learned colleague, Ms McMurrey, you confirmed that you arrived from Hadzici to Bradina on 8th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr Gligorevic, that on 9th May the units of the JNA and Serbian forces took over the centre of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. We were not listening to anything in Bradina. There was no electricity, so I did not know what was going on and when things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But if these were undisputed facts, you do not challenge them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply say I don't know anything about it, so I can neither confirm or contest it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Hadzici throughout the war until the NATO air strikes and the Dayton Agreement, it was controlled by Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 you were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in Hadzici then.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that in Hadzici there was the largest ammunition depot of the JNA in Duronica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, a little while ago you marked on the map the villages of Tarcin and Pozaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these are two local communes in the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that if the village of Hadzici was occupied and Bradina blocked, that Pozaric and Tarcin were in some kind of a sandwich, and unable to reach Sarajevo or Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This main road, yes, it is probably true for the main road, but they could go to some other roads.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, in relation to your answer, can you confirm that from Tarcin to Konjic you can reach that location in a car in half an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact time, but probably it is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the latter case to reach Konjic you have to go on the Macedon road through Fojnica and Djusina and it would take up at least fifteen hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that area. I can't tell you what is the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, as a teacher of the geography of the region --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would never ever go to Fojnica and I was never in that area so I really cannot tell you whether one needs 15 or 30 or 2 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You testified before this court that because of your poor eyesight you did not do your national service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said to my learned colleague that despite that you are able to see some persons even without your glasses and certain objects that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It depends on the distance where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were exempt from serving national service in the JNA in times of peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the case of war you would have to go to be examined by the commission and for your ability to be determined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know nothing about such a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr Gligorevic, that in April 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina the state of imminent danger of war was proclaimed? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to remember that. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The schools ceased to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They used to work on and off for a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time the general mobilisation was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr Gligorevic, that you did not respond to the call-up for the mobilisation in your municipality of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In case such a thing was proclaimed, I did not respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also when you arrived in Bradina, you did not respond to the call-up for mobilisation in the Territorial Defence headquarters in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct. There was no possibility to go to Konjic and nobody called me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not go to see a doctor for your inability to serve to be determined in the case of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not. Thank you. I would now like to ask you about one part of your statement given to the prosecutor. If you remember, Mr Gligorevic, last year you stated that in Bradina there was a meeting held between the inhabitants and the representatives from Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that. I was not present but I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated then that this meeting was joined by certain officials in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on that occasion you said that the meeting was attended by Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, the Chairman of the Municipality and Chairman of the War Presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I was told by my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also told that the meeting was attended by Jasmin Guska, the chief of the public security station, Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was also attended by Hanza Janovic, an officer, former JNA, who was at that time a member of the TO headquarters in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the meeting in Bradina that took place before I came from Hadzici, I was told he attended it. The second meeting, which took place at Podorasac, I can't tell you. I don't know whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know at that time it was demanded that the barricades and checkpoints from the main route be removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was told more or less at that last meeting that there was an agreement as the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was very bad and nothing was solved yet to wait for some kind of a political decision and for any side not to attack anybody. The meeting took place on the Saturday and in the meantime they were preparing an attack while they were trying to convince the people from Bradina they were not attacking them and the attack started on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the attack started on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told it was a Saturday. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the town of Konjic was shelled also on 23rd and on 24th and 25th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know for sure. We are some 12 or 13 kms away from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Gligorevic. There are just a few questions to confirm and clarify some things that you also stated before this court. You said that among the groups on the 27th from Bradina to Celebici were transported Petko Gligorevic and Miljanic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated before this Tribunal that Pero Gligorevic and Gojko Miljanic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name is Petko.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Gojko Miljanic died several hours later in the morning from the injuries they received on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, you also stated that after several days after your arrival to Hangar Number 6 a group from Tunnel Number 9 were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group from Bradina that was taken -- that was brought there the day before I arrived on 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed that some of them had bandages on their heads. I think it was Mirko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that before their arrival to the Hangar Number 6 these people were given medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know in what way and who gave them assistance. Among the people who were arrested there was also a doctor, Relja Mrkajic. He was also from Bradina. He was the one who gave medical assistance. I do not know who gave him all the bandages and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate before their arrival to hangar Number 6 they were given medical assistance, as you could see yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people had bandages on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated, and let me now clarify that, that several days later a group of Serbs arrested in Bjelasnica arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell this court whether there was a group of Serbs who from Bradina to Bjelasnica set off towards the Serb controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also state that these people had been beaten on the occasion of their arrest and when they were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In fact, that group which was brought there was put into Number 9, Tunnel Number 9, not in Hangar 6. So I saw them when they were transferred to Hangar 6.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You learned about that group from the persons transferred from Number 9 to Hangar Number 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among those transferred to Hangar Number 6 were some relatives of yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether there were any close relatives of mine but here was also my brother-in-law who was there, but not in the same group. He was brought from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just two more questions, Mr Gligorevic. Was among the group Pero Mrkajic, and was it correct that he was beaten very badly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in that group. Pero Mrkajic was brought with another group. He was very severely beaten. He was lying down next to me. He died of his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Gligorevic, can you tell me if you know if this group in which Pero Mrkajic was, that they captured near the village of Ljuta two members of the Territorial Defence and they subsequently killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You believe that other persons in that group can testify about that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in case that killing happened, I suppose this was not Pero's group. These were elderly people. Pero Mrkajic and somebody by the name of Djordjic. These were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you refer to Rajko Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which group up mean and where those killings took place but I know for Pero it was not him. He told me that later on, although he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate you did hear that some members were killed near the village of Ljuta on the road towards Kalinovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Nobody told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms Residovic. I think the Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inform your Honours that Mr Gligorevic has a plane waiting for him to travel back to the country where he lives. I have just one or two questions in re-direct to ask to him, so I would be very grateful on behalf of him if I could be allowed to do that and then the break may be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sorry to interrupt my learned friend, Mr Ostberg. There is a matter I want to raise privately with counsel for Mr Delalic. It concerns this witness and before he is released from cross-examination, I wonder whether I might beg your indulgence just to have a word privately with Mr O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: While the questioning is on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If your Honours thought that was not disrespectful to you, I would happily do that, if I might. It is a matter that has arisen out of the cross-examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As long as you whisper, that is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I promise to whisper. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, may we have a five minute break? It seems that I have may have missed a question? Can you allow me to consult for two or three minutes in order to complete my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hope I am not thought to have started a trend. Your Honour, this is a matter that arose out of something that Judge Jan raised this morning in relation to the specimen signature that was given, that one purpose to which that might be put would be comparison with the document which has been disavowed by this witness. It is a practical matter. My experience is that handwriting experts will need more than one specimen signature for purposes of comparison. I certainly know that in my jurisdiction a competent handwriting expert would need at least 12, but preferably 20 specimen signatures. I wonder whether the court would think it proper to ask the witness if before he leaves for his plane, and I have heard Mr Ostberg say he has to catch it, he might be asked to provide a sheet of A4 paper with 20 specimen signatures upon it and that should become part of the exhibits in the court in the way the other one did as well. I do not know whether it is, in fact, proposed to have it compared, but if there is any prospect of that, that ought to be done in order for an effective comparison to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He can be made to sign such a specimen signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: For that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope that is a helpful suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the prosecutor should make him sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ensure that he does it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before he catches the plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, before I leave this place, can I ask you to repeat which of the documents that I tendered are already accepted as defence exhibits and which have only been marked for identification purposes? If you could help me with that so that we know where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It should be clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, we are just trying to clear up. I think she had some of them offered for exhibit but she did not offer it into evidence and I would like for her to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought you were talking about the January 14th January 1993. He said the signature resembled his and probably he did not sign them. That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The only document which I can remember which could have been admitted is that dated 6th June 1993, which he wrote himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. She did not say the magic words of offering it into evidence. So that is what we were trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think she mentioned the number of the exhibit also. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. Thank you very much. So the documents that I have offered into evidence were accepted by the Trial Chamber and the documents that I asked to be marked for identification purposes as seen in the transcript were indicated as such. I thank my colleagues. Probably my way of tendering evidence is not so technically precise. So I thank them for the suggestion. I would also like to ask you, your Honours, bearing in mind that the witness spoke about his eyesight, if you could allow me to ask the witness to take off his glasses for a moment. Mr Gligorevic, can you see -- my colleague will now show --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you turn on the witness' microphone? You have to have your microphone on. Can you now please tell what you saw; what my colleague, Miss McMurrey, showed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She raised her hand with four fingers.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the witness saw four fingers. He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I object to this eye examination in open court. We cannot have this. He has answered questions about his eyesight and what he could see with and without glasses. I think this is ridiculous and should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, Ms Residovic, why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Madam Residovic, I do not know. It is up to you. You can ask him the number of glasses which he uses, but I leave it to you. I do not want to ... MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, can you please tell us what your eyesight is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have to wonder what happened so many years ago about eyesight. It deteriorates over the years. Even if it was good then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I purposely left it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not worth it. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. I have one more question for confirmation. Mr Gligorevic, in your statement given to the Prosecutor last year you stated that when you were taken to Celebici that Mirsad Musinovic, Rale, was the camp commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I was told but I did not know that man because I did not use to live in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer is that is what you were told and you did not know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him. The first time I saw him was at Musala, when he was a prisoner just as I was.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much once again and thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not go into a long re-direct examination. For the record I would please ask Ms Residovic to put on the ELMO the original of his own handwriting which was admitted as evidence to the court. We never got an exhibit in original. So could you please put it on the ELMO. It is the statement of 6th June 1993. If it is still there, maybe it can be put by the usher. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I apologise, your Honours. I did not have my earphones on, so I did not understand the suggestion of Mr Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No problem. It is just the document of 6th June 1993 now being put on the ELMO. You see it and recognise it, Mr Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please tell the court the circumstances and for what purpose you gave this handwritten statement in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot about this. Probably that was when the Red Cross was coming, the International Red Cross, that is. I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who did you give it to? Who took it from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that now exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: One thing I did not understand when you answered questions asked by Ms Residovic. You said something about why you named a gun in your paper. I did not understand your answer quite clearly. Why did you put that into the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, because that judge, or let us call him a judge, he was asking questions himself and answering the same questions and jotting them down.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are you now talking about what happened in Celebici, when you gave your statement there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you gave this statement, were you then reminded of the other statement you had already given in Celebici or signed in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object to him leading the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your interests are being protected. I do not know why you should bother. That is not re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. I think I have got the answers I was after to try to get. Thank you, your Honours. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 12 o'clock. I think that is all for this witness except for his specimen signatures, which he should hand over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Signatures, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. The Prosecution calls Nedeljko Draganic. Nedeljko Draganic (sworn)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May the witness be seated now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): My name is Nedeljko Draganic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How old were you in 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was 19 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: That makes you how old now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 23.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In 1992 were you working or were you in school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in school.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In May of 1992 specifically where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living at Cerici, which is a village next to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the usher put Prosecution Exhibit number 4, a map, on the ELMO, so that the ... Sir, I am going to ask if looking at the map that is to your right, not the one directly in front of you but this one, if you can show the court where Konjic is and then where Cerici is -- Konjic town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) Konjic is here and Cerici is here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. About how many houses were in Cerici in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, but there were some 40 households.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who is the ethnic background of most of the inhabitants of Cerici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a time when there was military action in or against your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there ever a time when there was any fighting or an attack or any sort of military action involving your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the Muslim Croat army started to attack on the 19th, and that they started to shell the village either on the 19th or 20th. I am not that sure of the date. Mostly it was only shelling. The inhabitants were mostly sheltered.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say 19th or 20th, can you tell us what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th or the 20th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you part of any armed defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you armed prior to the military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please very briefly describe what happened and whether or not you were arrested or captured following the military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was captured on 23rd May 1992 after all the shelling done by the Muslim Croat coalition. After that they entered the village once that all the villagers had left. I think they left on 22nd. I'm not too sure about dates. After that the Muslim Croat army entered the village, and all the men and women were taken to a field, Cerici field, in front of the house of Branko Sudar. We were all rounded up there and I was brought there from my house, which is 150 metres away from the house of Branko Sudar, where we were all brought. From there we were all transferred to Celebici. Then we were told that we were going for some kind of an informative interview and that we get back home by that evening, but we stayed there for three months.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say that all the men and the women were taken to a field and then "we were brought to Celebici", can you clarify exactly who it was that was brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The women and children were released and left to go home. They were told they can freely return to their houses, and there were some 17 of us, 16 or 17 -- I don't know the exact number -- maybe 15 of us. Yes, there was a group of us between 15 and 18 people, who were taken to Celebici. Most of us -- I mean, none of us had any weapons. I think that maybe two people had some hunting type of weapons with a permit for those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you brought when you were taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, we entered through the gate, and after that we were lined up against a wall, the wall that was in front of Tunnel Number 9. Right next to the gate there is a very big wall.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were searching us. They told us to take our shoelaces out of our shoes. They took our personal IDs, and searching us mostly. We had to face the wall and not to turn around, to stand still and to hold our arms up and against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then what happened next? Were you brought somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then after maybe an hour or an hour and of a half -- I don't know exactly -- then we were put into Tunnel Number 9 and that's where we spent that night.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Tunnel Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think for some three nights and two to three days. I do not know for sure, but anyhow when people from Bradina were brought in -- I think I was in Number 9 from 23rd May 1992 up until 26th May. I do not know exactly whether it was the night from 25th to 26th or the night from 26th to 27th May 1992, whether it was on one of these two days when they brought the prisoners from Bradina it was at that moment that we were transferred. I do not know into what -- what was the number of the building, but it was opposite the command building. They used to call it an infirmary. It used to be some kind of a fire station. There was fire-fighting equipment in that storage and those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back to your first two or three nights in Tunnel Number 9, can you please describe Tunnel Number 9 for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tunnel Number 9, when you enter it, there are two to three steps. It is right next to the main wall. When you enter through the gate, there is this main wall and this tunnel is right next to it. There are two or three steps. After that there is an iron door with a very small window in that door. That tunnel has got a slight inclination, a slope, that leads to another door, but I never went to the end of the tunnel. The tunnel is 1.5 metres large and it is high -- its height is about 2 metres and it is some 20 metres long. I'm not too sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were there, was the tunnel lighted? Was the tunnel lit -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Never while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were there approximately how many prisoners were in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The group that came with me, we were there in it some 16 or 17 people. Later on some other people were brought in, but I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask the technical support people to show on the computer Prosecution Exhibit 1/45? It is photograph 45 on page 33. Sir, do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Tunnel Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I then ask for 1, page 34, picture 46? I ask, sir, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is also Tunnel Number 9. The picture was made from the bottom end of the tunnel and one can see the door, which is open, and also the window I just mentioned, the window that's on the door.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the tunnel, were you ever formally interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was interrogated by Stenek. He was a police inspector of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were calling us out, to go out of the tunnel one by one, and they would be taking us in front of the command building. In fact, it was behind the command building. How shall I explain that? The northern side behind the command building. There was some kind of a table there and a guard was standing next to it. The guard was rather bigger type of man. He was, yes, rather big and he was some kind of a civilian police or military police -- I don't know. Then Stenek started to ask questions. He asked me who I was, what I was. He asked me what was going on in Cerici and Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you give a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was giving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, Miss McHenry. You have a big model here. Why do you not use that also? I find that none of the witnesses are being asked to indicate the places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a fair point. In fact, I was planning on asking him to use the model as well as a diagram, but, in fact, this is a fine time to do it. If I could have, first, the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has talked about the wall. He can indicate the wall, the location of the tunnel, all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would ask that this diagram, the original be marked for identification purposes and then put on the ELMO. It is, I believe, Prosecution Exhibit 86. The defence already has a copy of this. This is the diagram attached to the witness' statement. Your Honours, this is both a diagram and then I am going to also ask him to use the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He can indicate the wall he has talked about, the position of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The fact that the microphone does not allow someone to go to the model is slightly problematic, but ... Sir, I am showing you what has been marked for identification purposes as Prosecution Exhibit 86. Do you recognise this as a diagram you created in 1995 during an interview with people from the Office of the Prosecutor? If you want, you may look to your right, if that is easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I drew this when they came to see me for me to give a statement to them. This is a diagram of Number 6 and of number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to ask you to look in front of you to what has been admitted as Prosecution Exhibit 2 and ask if you recognise that as a model of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
