utterances.text: If the usher could show him the pointer, sir, if you could stand up and hopefully just from where you are standing, using this pointer, and if you can get to it from your seat, you can move around to the outside, but if you can reach over and just -- can you just start, show where the gate of the camp is and where Tunnel Number 9 is and where the wall is that you have already talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gate is here. The tunnel is somewhere here. As I can't see too well from here -- the tunnel is somewhere here. Number 6 is this and this here is Number 7. Here is the command building. This is where the guard post was, and here I was interrogated for the first time by Stenek. There was a table placed here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where is the wall that you were put against when you first arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is the shed that you went to when you left Tunnel Number 9, the building? I believe you said it stored fire-fighting equipment and was called the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going back to your interrogation, I believe I had asked if you had given a statement at that time. Would you please explain what, if anything, happened during your interrogation and whether or not you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave some kind of a statement, but I can't remember. The question was whether I had a rifle. I remember saying that I did not have a rifle. He also asked me other things concerning Donje Selo, and I do not remember what I answered. When I say Donje Selo, I include Cerici in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was that the only time while you were at Celebici that you were ever taken out and asked questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. How do you mean whether it was the only time? When they were beating me, they would sometimes ask some questions, some stupid things.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I will ask about that later to clarify. Thank you. Can you please describe how long -- you have indicated you were brought to the building across from the command centre. How long did you remain in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall very well. I can't tell exactly. It might have been -- I really do not know when I was transferred into Hangar 6. I think that I was transferred some time in June, June 1992, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were in this building, was it used as an infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly the conditions when you were in this shed, the building that was later used as an infirmary? Can you describe what that was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were almost non-existent. That means that we slept on the concrete. In case somebody had a jacket, he could put it on the floor and then lie down on it. There were quite a few of us there, so we slept so that one person would have his legs over somebody else's legs and then the third person would put his head over these legs. There were quite a few people in it and the conditions were, yes, almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: While you were in the shed, were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. You are talking about the shed? You are still talking about the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You do not know when he moved to the shed, from the hangar or whatever it is. We do not know when he moved out of the hangar. He is still talking about the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are talking about the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. THE JUDGE: You used the word "shed". Was it a shed or was it a building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It was a building, which I will refer to as the infirmary just for clarification, although I know it was not used as an infirmary while you were first there. While you were in this building, later used as an infirmary, were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on one occasion. I was taken out by Delic in front of the building. His leg was injured. I don't know what caused it. He was walking with crutches. He was waving these crutches and a shovel on to me, and he was shouting: "Where is now ...." He was mentioning a name, I think Boro Golubovic, and he said: "Do you want me to say where he is?" That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know Delic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only knew him from sight. I never met him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know his name before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please describe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man no hair, slightly bald. He's a rather big man, maybe 1.90 metres or 1.95 metres tall. He's got a very rounded and full face, a slightly larger head. He was very heavily built.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that you first saw Mr Delic in Celebici approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been maybe two or three days after I was transferred from Number 9 to this building. I don't know what you call it.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The building that was later used as an infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that when the incident you have just described, where he brought you out and asked you about a person, was that two or three days afterwards or was that another incident -- another time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it was quite soon, maybe two or four days after I was transferred from Number 9 to this building that they called the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was Mr Delic's role in the camp, as far as you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I could observe, he was some kind of a commander. Whether he was a guard commander or something like that ...

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How is it that you observed that he was some kind of commander? What kinds of things did you observe leading to your conclusion that he was some sort of commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to what the guards said and from what I could observe when he was talking to some guards, this is basically on what I base my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see him give instructions to anyone or did you ever see him take instructions from other guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him give orders to guards.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, did you observe anyone else having authority over the guards or over the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my entire stay in the camp, I don't know, except if one could think that the person who released me from the camp was in charge. I don't know what his function was.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was the person who released you from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know him before you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see him while you were present in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw him once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was that you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear other guards or other people in authority refer to Mr Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe the guards would mention him from time to time, but I did not hear much about him.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever become aware that he was present in the camp, even if you yourself did not see it -- did not see him physically, for instance from things you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even if you yourself did not see Mr Mucic other than the couple of occasions you have told us about, were there other occasions when you were aware that he was in the camp, although you personally did not see him during those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you brought after you were taken out of the building that later became the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where approximately did you sit in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the chart that I drew, and I sat here, where this indication number 1 is. This is approximately where I sat (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what the conditions were like when you were in Hangar Number 6, and if you want to use your diagram while you are explaining things, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were bad. There were many people there, many people in Hangar Number 6. There were about 250, maybe 240 people. The number was not the same all the time, because some people would leave and other people would come in. So I don't know. People sat next to the sheet metal walls. That's the row around here all the way down next to the walls (indicating), and there were two rows in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you just again show where approximately among these people was your place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did you sleep and what kind of facilities were given to you for sleeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I slept here on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What were conditions like in the hangar when it was hot outside or when it was raining outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it was hot outside, it was very hot inside the hangar, because it was painted green and it got really very hot, and when it rained, the row next to this wall, there was some kind of a sliding door there. They were all in water. They couldn't sleep at all, because everything got wet. Everything they had got wet, so they couldn't sleep because they were in the water.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of food and toilet facilities there were when you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received food. We usually received a slice of bread. A loaf of bread, which was the normal size, would be sliced into 16, 18 or 19 slices. That's how they sliced it up. Then sometimes they would bring some kind of vegetables stew. Then after that you could get about two or three spoonfuls of vegetable stew. We all ate from one bowl and everybody else ate from the same bowl and we used the same spoons. I think there were five spoons and so five of us would go out and we would eat three or four spoonfuls and that was it. That was the food that we received.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you receive food every day while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. There were days where we wouldn't receive any food.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you remember, what was the longest period of time you ever went without being given any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was you went three or four days without getting food? What month, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in July. I am not sure but I believe it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. What kind of toilet facilities were there for the people in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had some kind of a hole that had been dug up and there was a plank across it. It was located here and when we had to go to the toilet, we had to ask the guard to let us go and they usually allowed us to go there in groups to urinate and also when we had to have our bowel movements. So we had to go there. Usually two of us would go to defecate and as for urination, we usually did that next to the ditch. We pissed inside this ditch and the water flowed and took it away.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you: is it also the case -- were there guards stationed outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I ask, using the model, that you both show the toilet facilities you were talking about and where the guards were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) The toilet was somewhere here, somewhere here, and the guards were posted at first here. They were somewhere here, whether here or there. It depended on the shift on the number of guards, two or more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were available to the guards who were guarding the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a machinegun and they had rifles. I guess they were automatic rifles. I do not know if they had any semi-automatic rifles. Maybe. At first they kept a machine gun here and then they moved it here.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. During the time that you were in the camp, were you ever told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never told personally what was the reason for my capture, but Delic walked into the Hangar Number 6 on one occasion and he told us that we are detained because we were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever mistreated, sir, while you were being kept in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the first time that you remember being mistreated? And I ask that you speak very slowly so that the interpreters can interpret what you are saying and that you explain to us everything that happened, please, slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was taken out from Hangar Number 6 and I was called out by Zenga Landzo -- I don't know his first name -- Osmo Dedic -- yes, Osmo Dedic, Adis Alikadic. I think there was a fourth person with him. I think he was called Lisko or something like that. They called me out and they took me to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that the hangar next to Hangar 6 that you previously pointed out on the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Indicating) It's the one down there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they led me in hangar Number 7 and they tied me to a beam so that I was standing up but my hands were tied up above my head. Then they started beating me using all kinds of things. They were kicking me and hitting me with planks and rifle butts and then they asked me where my rifle was. I did not have a rifle. I kept telling them that I didn't have a rifle. They kept beating him until I lost consciousness. When I fainted, they started telling me: "Get up." When I fainted, I was suspended hanging on my hands. After that the four of them -- I don't know for how long they beat me, maybe half an hour. Four of them brought me back to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, who was it exactly who was beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion I was beaten by Landzo, nicknamed Zenga; Osman Dedic; Adis Alikadic; and Lisko -- I think that his name was Lisko -- the four of them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case, sir, that all four of them participated in the actual beating of you, in actually hitting you with their hands or with the instruments that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now you have mentioned Landzo nicknamed Zenga. Did you know him before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from the town. We went to the same high school and I also knew him from the cafes in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What is his age compared to your age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have been my age or maybe a year younger, maybe 18, 17 at that time in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you know his name before you were at the camp, either his nickname or his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his last name, because they called him Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In the camp what was he referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was called Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anyone else called Zenga when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you know, what does "Zenga" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the term used for Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know what term in the Croatian army would result in someone being called "Zenga"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the national guard corps, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. What are the initials in Serbo-Croatian for national guard corps, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe what Zenga Landzo looked like in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was about 1.75, 1.80 metres tall. He had a crew cut. In fact, he was shaven at the sides and just maybe 2 mms of hair on the top of his head. His face was -- it was slightly elongated and he had a specific voice actually, a peculiar accent.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he ever wore anything on top of his head, any sort of head covering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He usually wore a green beret.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, to your knowledge was Zenga there the entire time you were at Celebici or did there come a time when he left Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that maybe in August -- he was there most of the time but I'm not sure whether he was there for the entire duration of the 90 days that I spent in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was it that you left Celebici, just the date, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late August, maybe on 30th, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Was the occasion you just told us about the only occasion when Zenga mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was the person who abused me the most in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you can, can you approximate how many times he physically mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten times or more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you remember the second time that you were mistreated by Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the order of the incidents but I do know that the first time when I was beaten -- I know about the first time but as for the order of the other events ... the only thing I can tell you is that I was beaten very often. I don't know the exact order of the beatings, what happened the second time, what happened the third time and the fourth time and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Would you then, please, just tell us specifically about another incident where you were mistreated by Zenga, even if you do not know where it was in the exact order, but I want you at this time just to tell us about one specific incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I was taken out at night by Zenga and Osman Dedic. They beat me right in front of Number 7 on the lawn here. They beat me here I don't know for how long. I think that I fainted two or three times and then I would come to again and faint again. Then I was brought back to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there anything during that incident in particular that resulted in your being brought back? Did something happen that resulted in you being brought back to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to the leading form of her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to the incident that you have just been telling us about, besides the fact that you were being beaten and you lost consciousness several times, is there anything else that you remember about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that Zenga grabbed me by the hair and dragged me on the asphalt, and I fell down, but he kept pulling me up by my hair, and he dragged me to the entrance door and threw me in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there any other -- your Honour, is this a good time to stop before we start with another incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. We may as well have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will resume at 2.30, when you continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we now continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Before we continue, I would like to notify the video registrar people that at some point in the near future I will be asking them to potentially use this camera. I neglected to notify them of that before lunch. Thank you. Sir, in addition to the two incidents you described prior to lunch can you describe the next incident or another incident that you remember where you were mistreated by Zenga, Mr Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly remind him of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. That is a good idea, your Honour. The first incident is when he was brought to -- when you were brought to the hangar Number 7 and tied to the beam and the second incident is when you were brought outside the hangar in a grassy area and you were beaten by Mr Landzo and another person in your -- you were grabbed by your hair and lost consciousness. Besides those two incidents, can you please tell us about another incident that you remember, if any, where you were mistreated by Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He mistreated me on several occasions. In one of those occasions he took me out and told me to sit down in front of hangar Number 7. I had to sit down against the wall with my legs close together, and this is the way in which I raised my arms. The knees went upwards. It was here. Then he spilt petrol or something like that over me, or maybe it was alcohol. Then he spilt it over me and he tried to put fire, but his lighter did not work and at the end he used a match, and he burnt both my legs, and he did not allow me to put the fire out until it was put out by itself, and my trousers were completely burnt out and both my legs had burnt and even today I have a scar on my left leg and it can't really be seen on my right leg.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of the technical support people may I ask you, sir, would you mind showing the Chamber and the defence attorneys the visible scar that still remains on your left leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I stand up and show it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How will he do it? It depends on what part of his legs?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is on, if I understand correctly, it is on his shin. I assume if you will just wait one minute, I believe somebody will come and be able to operate the camera. Your Honour, the court's indulgence for one second, please. While the video people are doing that, maybe I will just continue a little bit please and move forward. Sir, since you have been at the Hague, have any pictures been taken of your scars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance I would like to show you three photographs, which I would like marked as Prosecution exhibits 87, 88 and 89. These have previously been shown to defence counsel. May I have them marked for identification purposes first from the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Has he identified them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Not yet, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He should identify them. Then you can mark them. It is not you identifying them; it is he identifying them, not you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In general so the record is clear I thought it would be best to have them marked beforehand. Certainly they cannot be admitted into evidence. Sir, with respect to those photographs, can you tell me whether or not you recognise these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do recognise them. This is the picture of my left leg.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask the usher's assistance in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now he has identified you can have them identified, not when you got them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Have they been marked for identification purposes? Yes. May I ask that they be put on the ELMO? ? (Shown) the next photograph, please (shown). The final photograph, please (shown). At this time, up your Honours, I would ask that prosecution cues exhibits 87, 88 and 89 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any objections to its production.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No objection from the defence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I could now please ask for assistance from the technical support people so that the witness can show the court using the video camera his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we request permission to go look and examine the wound also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, may I ask that you stand up, please and you pull up your trouser leg. Does he need to go over to the camera? Can I ask, sir, that you come over towards the camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was waiting for him to pull his trouser leg up first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may resume your seat now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it only on one leg? I thought he had two.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe he had injuries on both legs but in terms of scars that are just remaining, it is only visible now on one injury. When he sits down, I will ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have one question on that. We have an agreement this was going to be examined by a doctor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. There was an application and I can verify with the witness, but I believe that -- I have not had a chance to verify with the witness -- he has been sent to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is an application by the defence for a medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think there was a joint application by Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The application I saw is a joint one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, from this burning you showed us one leg. Are there visible injuries on your other leg remaining at the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When approximately was it as best --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to try testing 1, 2, 3. Testing 1, 2, 3. Can you hear me now, sir. I don't know. Maybe we can try the other outlet. Sir, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you give us an approximate date when it was that Mr Landzo burnt your legs, even a month if you don't recall the exact date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the date, but it happened somewhere towards the end of June or in early July.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please describe -- you have described how your leg was burnt and how the fire itself went out. What happened after the fire went out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, after the fire went out there was a blister that appeared, and after that it became infected and it was in a very bad state because of all the dust around. It was full of pus all the time and my leg was swollen and hurt.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long did your leg remain in this condition, infected and full of pus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until I was released, and I was released, I think, on 30th August, in late August; whether on 30th or 31st August I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you return to the hangar after you were burnt? Immediately after the burn happened did you return to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were the injuries on your leg visible to, for instance, other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were visible, but I was trying to hide them for quite some time. I was covering them with trousers because when I was going to the infirmary, to the place which they called the infirmary, in order to change the bandages -- I mean the building there, C, then Delic stopped me at the corner just in front of the building and he asked me what happened to my legs. At the same time Landzo was standing next to him, so I had to lie. I did not know what to answer, because he knew what happened, but he was simply provoking and asking me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long -- did you receive immediate medical care after you were burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please tell us about when it was that you received medical care and exactly what was done for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe some seven days later -- I am not sure -- I am quite sure it was about a week afterwards, and the two physicians, Dr Petko and Relja -- Dr Petko -- I don't know his surname, and as Dr Relja Mrkajic were there. They were both physicians from Konjic and they were in that infirmary -- I mean what the people from the camp called the infirmary. They had some drugs there, so they cleaned the wound slightly, and whenever I would ask to go there so that they could clean the wound, very often Delic would not allow me to go. He often told me not to go and said: "You don't need that. You won't last very long".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did at any point either -- did Mr Mucic ask you how you received your injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In addition to now the three incidents you have described, are there any other specific incidents that you remember where you were mistreated by Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would beat me almost every day, but the very severe beatings, that also happened on many occasions. One of the -- one of his types of behaviour towards all of us detainees at Celebici, he would take us out to piss and when people would go out to piss, he ordered the others to drink it, and I was one of those who had to drink that. He would force us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The times that Mr Landzo would mistreat you, besides the ones you have already told us about, would he use any instruments or would it just be with his --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to her leading form of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Sustained, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the proper question is what happened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us in what manner you were beaten on the other occasions by Mr Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would usually beat me with a baseball bat. The bat used for playing baseball. He would usually beat me and the other detainees at the camp. He would beat me in front of Hangar 7, the hangar I showed to you before. He would beat me with a baseball bat there. I can't remember how many times. I can't even remember that. He used to take me out two or three times per day to beat me, all in the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: You have mentioned before Mr Delic. Was Mr Delic ever present during your mistreatment or did he ever mistreat you himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr Delic was present when Landzo was beating me in front of Hangar 7 in that grassy area in front of Number 7. Let me just stand up. Zenga beat me here and Delic was standing here and was looking at how Landzo was beating me. Delic told him at some stage to stop or something like that and then Zenga stopped beating me and then he told him to take me back. Delic also -- Delic never took me out to beat me, but when he would walk into Hangar Number 6 where we were sitting down on the concrete, and then with a baseball bat he would come and hit, whether every person or every other person it did not matter, but anyway whenever he would pass by me he would hit me at least twice or more. It was only one time that he passed me by without hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have previously described both Mr Delic and Mr Landzo. I am asking you: since you have come to The Hague here to testify were you shown two series of photographs and asked whether you recognised anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was what you said when asked this question written down and then later signed by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an exhibit to show. In my system I would normally have it marked before being shown to the witness but if I understand your Honours correctly, you would like me to show it to the witness first and then have it marked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the better procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. This has previously been provided to defence counsel. You can just show it to him and I have extra copies for the court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to object for the record. We do not have any objections to the way the photo-spread was presented, but we believe that the photo identification of Mr Landzo is invalid because the witness has already testified that he knew him from high school. They went to the same high school together, so I do not see what the purpose of it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If the defence counsel wishes to stipulate that the witness was able to recognise Mr Landzo, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually is identity in issue? Mr Landzo's identity, is it in issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Not according to the Prosecution, but since we do not know exactly what the defence is, if the defence wishes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness says he knows him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He says he knows him, your Honour, and I believe that is confirmed by everyone, including Mr Landzo. They were in the same school; not necessarily in the same class but in the same school. That is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If defence counsel wishes to stipulate that identification is not an issue with respect to this witness, then I will withdraw the entire exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We will stipulate that he knew him from before and so there is no problem with him recognising him from Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is unnecessary to have them on the record then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Before I proceed further, let me just ask with respect to Mr Delic if defence counsel wishes to stipulate that the witness knew Mr Delic from before and you could recognise him; otherwise I will continue with another photo-spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think any stipulation -- before what? Knew him before what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before he went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Whether or not the defence will agree that the witness was able to recognise Mr Delic at the camp and subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We will stipulate to that, that he can recognise Mr Delic's -- that he can recognise Mr Delic as the person who was at the camp. We will stipulate to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That he could recognise Mr Delic, yes. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know why you want these photographs at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had not been sure exactly what the defence would and would not challenge, but with these I do not believe it is necessary, so I will not ask that they be admitted into evidence, given the stipulations. Sir, while you were in the camp, did you yourself observe any incidents where the persons -- did you witness any murders, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you know about the first murder that you remember, and if you can, please tell us approximately when it was this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it very well when the late Simo Jovanovic was called out from Hangar Number 6. He was taken out and he was beaten for at least some forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object to no personal knowledge. He can testify the witness was taken out of the hangar, but once the witness is taken out of the hangar he has not witnessed anything of the sort. He can testify as to his condition when he was taken out and his condition when he was brought back in, but he has no personal knowledge about what occurred outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought that is what he was testifying to, the condition when the person was brought in or if he was never brought in again. This type of testimony is expected of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He says he was taken out and beaten for at least 40 minutes. I am saying he was testifying from no personal knowledge there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we ask him how much he knew he was being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the point from where he is continuing. Where is he continuing from?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Sir, with respect to Mr Jovanovic, who was it who took him out of the hangar, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he was called out by Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He said he heard he was called out by Zenga. Did he see or hear Zenga himself. If he has no personal knowledge, then he cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Were you there when he was called out? Were you there when he was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you hear the voice of the person who called him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard Zenga's voice.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Once the person was taken out what, if anything, did you hear or observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat him there. There were several of them. They beat him and he was moaning and he was crying: "Please don't do it, brothers".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He can testify to what he hears, but since he was taken out of the hangar, he does not know who was out there, what was happening. So he is testifying from no personal knowledge about what happened outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How did you know he was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat him maybe 10 metres away from the door so that we could hear his moans and we heard everything. We heard him say: "Please don't do it, brothers" and we could hear the blows. I don't know what they used to beat him. Then after that he was carried in. They called some people to go out and to bring him in, and I know that he was dead in the morning, because I carried him out together with Cedo Cecez and somebody else. I don't know who it was. I don't remember his name. I just know that Cedo Cecez and myself were also there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you could hear the moans and the blows could you recognise the voices of anyone else besides the victim, Mr Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could recognise the voice of Landzo and no other voices. The others were unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that he was dead in the morning and you carried him out, is that the next morning after he was taken out and then returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taken -- carried out at night, maybe at 10 pm. We didn't know what the time was. Maybe it was even 12. I'm not sure. Then in the morning when we got up that man was lying there dead at his place.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was who brought him back in after he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there any other murders that you have information from your own personal knowledge about in addition to Mr Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a murder that happened in front of all of us. They beat an old man. I don't know his name. I know that he had two sons there and a brother. He was an elderly man, maybe about 60 years old. He was small, maybe 1.70 metres tall, and he had grey hair and he was from Bradina. He was killed in front of all of us. They beat him. Zenga was in that group. He was the one who beat him the most. He fell down. I think he was in a coma. Then the prisoner sitting next to me, he was some kind of a nurse. He was doing in a lab -- he was doing blood analysis. He jumped up and pulled out his tongue. Then later on they transferred him to the medical area and we heard that he died there in the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When this man was being beaten what was being used to beat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They have used everything. They beat him with planks, rifle butts. They punched him, they kicked him. They used all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Apart --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even a baseball bat. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately when did this beating occur, if you know? What month or when in the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was around St Peter's day, 12th July, because I think that this was the time when some Muslim police officers were killed in the Bradina area, and then they started to beat the people from Bradina very severely. Muslims thought that some Serbs from Bradina who remained in the wood, that they had killed those Muslim police officers. I don't know what kind of police it was. I think it was the military police unit. Then after that they beat the people from Bradina very severely, and that was the time when this elderly man died as a consequence of the beating.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are there any other murders, sir, that you have personal information about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was the murder of Zjelko Klimenta, nicknamed Keljo. He was taken out in the morning around 6 or 7am. It was in the early morning. The dawn had just broken and the sun wasn't out yet but you could see very well it was already light. He was taken out with a group of other detainees and they talked for a while, and then all of a sudden there was a shot and a man walked back in and they said: "Keljo was killed".

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When approximately was Keljo killed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early morning, maybe around 6.00 am.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know what month it was or approximately what period of time when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe ten days or two weeks before the arrival of the Red Cross, and the Red Cross arrived on 12th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, where were you at the time that the Red Cross came? Were you in Hangar Number 6 when the Red Cross came to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was in the infirmary, as they called it.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long had you been at the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few days and then I was taken back to Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When were you -- am I correct that a few days before the Red Cross came you were moved to the infirmary? Did I understand you correctly about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then how long did you remain in the infirmary before you were moved back to Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I am not sure now -- I think it was about a day or two after the Red Cross left.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked us -- that was the usual procedure: first name, last name, date of birth, things like that. We had to fill in some forms and then later on there was a French woman. She was a doctor, and she examined my wounds. She examined my wounds and they noted down my statement. I gave a statement to the Red Cross. They asked me what had happened and I told them everything that had been done to us, what happened to my legs. Then when the Red Cross left the camp, I think that Delic ordered Shiptar, an Albanian person, who was a cook there, and Zenga to -- in fact, I think that Zenga was not in the camp at that time. There was this Albanian man and a man from Forjak, who was also a guard there. He ordered them to beat me. They beat me. Let me just indicate the location. They beat me here at this corner and Delic stood here, right in front of the command building. Again he said: "Enough" and they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when was it that you were released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was on 30th August 1992, but I am not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you please describe what happened during your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, they released a group before I was released, and then after maybe two hours they called out our names. They called out our names and called us to go out and to pick up our things, and I then went into an Iveco van. There was some kind of a mattress inside on which we sat. Then Pavo took all of us and his driver and we went to the Third March School so that we can be given release forms, that we had been released from the Celebici camp. Then after that Pavo and his driver drove us to the village of Bijelica. That is in Donje Selo. It is like a hamlet. The locals call it Bijelica or Ciba. I got out of the van there and Pavo gave me the certificate indicating that I had been released from the camp and that I had freedom of movement in the area of Cerici. This happened in front of either Zoran Cecez's house or Marko Cecez's house. This is where I was allowed to get off the van.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: After you were released did you ever see Mr Mucic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Under what circumstances did you yourself see Mr Mucic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean "circumstances"?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: For instance, where was it? Why was he there? Why were you there? Can you just explain a little bit about where it was and why it was that you saw Mr Mucic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sometimes came to see my parents in their house, and I also saw him sometimes when he passed by in his car.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you ever present when Mr Mucic was at your house and, if so, -- well, did you ever hear any of the conversation between Mr Mucic and anyone in your family, hear it yourself rather than be told it by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard personally.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to what you heard personally, what was the subject of the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked about a number of things, but mostly the discussion was about the release of some of our relatives from the camp, from the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: While you were present was there any discussion of anyone besides Mr Mucic being involved in the decisions to release prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that only on one occasion Pavo mentioned that he had to ask Delalic, because he was the Commander, his commander. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: One second, please. Your Honours, at this time I would move into evidence Prosecution Exhibit 86, which is the diagram that the witness had drawn and earlier used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just the one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, your Honour: I do not need it to be shown to the witness unless your Honours have any question. He previously identified it. Before I tender him for cross-examination, I just want to make sure the record reflects it has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It has been.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: In which order are you taking the witness? Let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: First will be counsel for Mr Delic; then counsel for Mr Landzo, followed by counsel for Mr Mucic and lastly counsel for Mr Delalic

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and, as you know, I am the defence lawyer for Hazim Delic. I am going to ask you a few questions and I would like you to listen to the questions and just answer the questions I ask, and we will be through this a lot quicker. Can you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you. Let me just start off at the beginning of your testimony. You said that in your village during the shelling the inhabitants were mostly sheltered. What did you mean by that? Did you have bunkers constructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no shelters that had been built but there was a part -- an area near Sudarif Podok. That is near the upper part of the village of Cerici, and there is a little dale next to a stream, and this is some kind of a natural shelter. Nobody had constructed any kind of shelters in Cerici, as far as I know. All the people were either there or in Malo Osoija, which is also a fairly wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Thank you very much. When you were first brought to Celebici were you beaten while you were searched at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: So basically all that happened is that you were checked into the camp. You were searched, valuables were taken from you and taken into custody and then you were moved to tunnel 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would be happy to. By the way, if I ask a question you do not understand, I would be happy to rephrase, it repeat it, whatever you makes you comfortable, sir. Basically when you were at the wall, right after you were brought to Celebici, what occurred was you were searched, valuables were taken from your custody and taken into the custody of someone else and you were basically just checked into the camp, and then moved to tunnel 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct, but I did not have any valuables on me. They didn't take any valuables from me. I just had my personal ID card and they returned that to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But if other people that were with you had valuables, those were taken into the custody of the guards; is that correct? What I am getting at is there was a routine essentially checking into a custody facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that anything was taken away from anyone else. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That is fine, sir. Now you were in tunnel 9 for a couple of days and then you were transferred to what you call the infirmary. I am just going to ask you a little bit about that building. It had some windows in it, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In the building that you refer to as the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were windows.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But they were not clear glass like the glass behind you. You could not see out them, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could see through them.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, sir. Then after you were in that building for several days you were then transferred to Hangar Number 6, and you testified at some length about the conditions in Hangar Number 6. I believe you either said in your testimony or you said in your statement that there were no blankets available; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall an incident or an occurrence where there were some detainees that had blankets and Mr Delic had the blankets cut up so that everyone, or as many people as could would have a piece of blanket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that for a time some people who went out to work to unload things that they brought back the blankets. I am not sure whether he did that. I can't confirm. I don't know. He have may have; he may have not. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: You just do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine. You also talked quite a bit about the food while you were in Hangar 6. Do you know whether the food was cooked in the camp or whether it was brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the rations that the guards were eating, how they compared with what you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody told us that at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Water in hangar 22. You either testified on direct examination or you said in your statement and I frankly do not remember which, that there was no water available. Is that not correct? That is what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't in Number 22. It was in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Number 6. I am sorry. There was -- while you were in Hangar 6 there were buckets of water that were available for the use of the detainees, were there not, to drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that there were there at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: You never saw any there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were buckets that people could use if they had to defecate or urinate. I don't know anything about any buckets with water.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You also testified on direct examination that a group of three guards or possibly four guards -- you only knew the names of three -- on several occasions beat you, and one of those guards was an Osman Dedic, D-E-D-I-C. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That was not Hazim Delic; they are two different people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: I wanted to clear that up because the names sounded similar and I wanted to ensure that the court understood they were two different folks. Your Honour, at this point I will pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Moran.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Draganic, my name is Cynthia McMurrey and I am a defence counsel obviously. You visited with the prosecution on October 23rd and October 25th in 1995, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Some time in 1995, that is the same time you drew the prosecution exhibit, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nodded.)

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You said also your profession is a computer programmer, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you work as a computer programmer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Given that this witness as far as I know -- is she asking about 1992 or now because if she is talking about now I object, because I do not believe it is appropriate that this witness' country, much less place of employment, be given.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I had assumed he was still working in the Konjic area I may be wrong, but I was assuming that and this was for impeachment purposes, because I have been informed that he really is not working as a computer programmer in that area. So I am asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Tell us where you are working as a computer programmer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are you working as a computer programmer in the Konjic area now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You are from Cerici, which is near Donje Selo, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In 1992, Cerici was all Serbian, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in the former Yugoslavia, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You had the right, because you were 18 years old in 1992, so you could have voted or did vote in the March 1st referendum, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which referendum?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There was a referendum on March 1st, 1992 in which the Bosnians voted to declare independence from Yugoslavia. Did you vote in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you could have voted, because the voting age in Yugoslavia was 18, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not vote.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The question was: but you could have voted, had you wanted to, could you not have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You also stated before that you were too young to be recruited into the military service in 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But, in fact, you were 19 years old in 1992 and there really is no minimum age limit for military service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and since I was at high school after I graduated from the high school, I was supposed to do my national service in the Yugoslav National People's Army, or had I enrolled at college, then I could have gone on to do my national service after my college. I don't know anything about any laws for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you are aware that after March 1st there was no more -- Bosnia was an independent country. It was not part of the Yugoslavia Republic, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object to that because it is assuming facts not in evidence. In fact, it is not correct that after March 1st --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am just asking him if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he knows, let him say. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were in school at the time, though, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe you were studying some kind of special mathematics school, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So as an intelligent, educated man, are you saying you did not read the newspaper; you did not listen to the news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not interested in politics. Even today I don't follow that. I'm not interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The truth it you stated you were too young to go into the military service, but you are actually older than Mr Landzo, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The thing is I was going to school at the time and according to the Yugoslav law, once you finish high school you go and do your service in the army, and in case you go to college or some kind of a university, you could postpone the national service and do it afterwards. I hope that is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but when Bosnia declared its independence and the shelling of the Konjic area started, there was no more school for you to attend right then, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any school any more.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the attack on Cerici began about May 19th or 20th; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested with other members of your family on May 23rd; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. You and your brother were arrested by a combination of forces. There were people from the military police, people from the HVO and people from the TO present, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you were arrested, you were arrested by the combined force of military police, Territorial Defence and the HVO, Croatian forces, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that there was any kind of military police there. There was only the HVO and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you were not aware that the military police drove through the town of Cerici and announced and asked the people to turn down their weapons peacefully, and they answered the military police by firing? You do not recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was on May 19th or 20th of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody shot five of them. Certainly not in Cerici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Not shot five of them; fired their weapons in response to the request for laying down their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I object and at least ask for clarification as to exactly whether or not the defence counsel is asking a question or providing information. If I could just have the exact question being asked of the witness clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will be happy to try. My question is: On May 19th or May 20th, 1992 you do not remember the military police driving through your village, announcing over a loudspeaker for you to lay your arms down peacefully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What answer do you expect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want him to say whether he remembers that or not. Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the type of question you ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object. She can ask if he knows or not. "Do you remember" first of all assumes it is a fact. I object to that. I do not object if she wants to ask the witness if he knows that happened, without assuming, in fact, it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you recall this happening at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Same objection. I would ask her if the witness knows if this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you have any memory of this happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he does, fine. If he does not, I am not stating a fact if he does not know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have no objection if she wants to ask if the witness knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this type of dialogue is unprecedented. Let me take the witness for you. You are being asked on the day your village was taken certain members of your community fired at the HVO and Territorial Army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear of that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you pursue this again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will proceed now. Thank you. You did know that many Serbs in your village were armed, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you knew your neighbour, Lazo Cecez from Donje Selo, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him. How can he be my neighbour if he lives 3 kms away from where I lived?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is Cerici really a suburb of Donje Selo? Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Cerici is a village apart. The only thing is that the local commune is the same. It's the same local commune, Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you know Lazo Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I used to know Lazo Cecez.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also knew that he was in charge of distributing the weapons to the Serbian villages of Donje Selo and Cerici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You do know that he was the husband of Grosdana Cecez, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The villagers of Donje Selo and Cerici were armed by the ex-JNA and the SDS forces, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, your father had a weapon in 1992, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your father did turn over his weapon to the TO, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You knew also that Miro Golubovic and Milovan Kuljanin, Mici, were armed, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, Milovan Kuljanin had a special weapon with a scope on it for sniping, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was a hunting sniper, not a military one.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Miro Golabovic had a semi-automatic rifle, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what he had.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you say that there was not any armed resistance of Cerici against the attack on May 19th and May 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know there was no attack, neither any -- nor defence. They were shooting and they asked the Territorial Defence from Cerici to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Cerici did not surrender until May 23rd, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Cerici surrendered earlier than that, I think on 22nd. It was the first village to surrender. Later on Ciba surrendered and then Donje Selo and then Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is obvious it took at least three or four days to liberate Cerici, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean to liberate Cerici?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I mean, to come in and capture the city. It took three to four days, did it not? If it started on May 19th and they surrendered, or you were arrested on May 23rd, how many days is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning on 23rd they entered when everybody who had any weapons surrendered their arms. Then they entered, the Muslim and the Croat troops, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But they began the attack on 19th or 20th, as you stated before; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the date, whether it was on 19th or the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, counsel, I think we will have to break and reassemble at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: (short break).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is still on his oath. Let him appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, your Honour. Mr Draganic, I just wanted to clarify something. We went through the dates of the attack on Cerici. You are not telling this court today that there was no attack on Cerici and that there was no defence, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
