utterances.text: That is not what I said. I said that they shelled. I mean, the Muslim Croatian coalition shelled Cerici for a full day, and that evening those people called from Cerici saying that they would surrender. Then they stopped shelling Cerici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you are telling this court too that you remember that there were weapons and bullets fired back at the people that were attacking Cerici; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You mean, you did not tell us earlier that there were people who were armed who did fire their weapons during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He did not say that. He did not. You suggested but he denied it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I thought he said it. Okay. So just for clarification, you are saying there was no defence of Cerici? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some kind of defence, but there was no firing: it was only them who shelled Cerici. The Muslim area was shelling Cerici, and after that the people from Cerici called them to surrender. If you think that this is an attack which was answered by some defence, I do not see it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Just one second, your Honour. Now you also said you had this mathematics background, did you not, and you stated on May 21ST your village was shelled and a shell fell about every 40 seconds, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A shell would fall every 40 seconds, but I am not sure about the date. I think it was 21st May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. So if a shell fell every 40 seconds on 21st May, that would be two days times 1 shell every 40 seconds, that would result in more shells than the number of shells that fell on Konjic for 1,000 days, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Multiplying it you get to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know? Calculations, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he claims there is one shell every 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: For how many hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He says for a full day. So 24 hours times 60 shells a minute, it is an outrageous amount of shells he is claiming. That is all I am trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say it lasted for 24 days. The shelling started in the morning and stopped in the evening when they called the telephone, the Territorial Defence, saying they would surrender. The shelling lasted for one day, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: A day of 24 hours or of 12 hours? It depends, because you can count a day morning to evening or morning to the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Let us say it is 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say it lasted for 12 hours. I said it started in the morning and ended in the evening. I do not know for sure how many hours it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am just taking an average day from sun up to sunset is probably about 12 hours. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is the one who made the statement about how much shelling occurred in one date. I am just trying to clarify and test his knowledge, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you pursue it if it is of no value to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it was an unreasonable statement for him to make. My purpose is impeach him with his own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What does it go to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It goes to the fact that he is making outrageous statements that cannot be fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the benefit to your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, just going about the whole thing about whether he is telling the truth about whether they were armed, whether they fired back. If he is not telling the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Anyway, I am finished with that. Then when you were arrested on May 23rd with your brother, you were beaten before you were taken to Celebici, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Going back a while ago, you did state that during the shelling the Muslim forces were shelling Cerici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say the Muslim forces. I said it was the coalition of Muslim and Croat forces that attacked Cerici together.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I am sorry. I did not get the answer. Were you beaten on your way to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You also stated when you arrived at Celebici and you were placed on the wall, you were not beaten at that time either, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You said you were taken to Tunnel Number 9 first. You did state that the only light in Tunnel Number 9 during the day was the window over the door or the light that came in over the door; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, and also when someone would open the door.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Also at night-time there was no light in Tunnel Number 9, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was never any light during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Also then after you were taken out of Tunnel Number 9 you were moved to the infirmary or building Number 22, or the shed. I am sorry. Were you not? You were moved to that little building next to the command centre, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after two to three days I was transferred from Tunnel Number 9 into the building that later on was called the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also know that in the infirmary there are just a few windows on the back, and they are covered with an opaque glass that cannot be seen through; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe he said he could not see out of it. I want to make sure it was an opaque glass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought he said he could see through it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Did you say you could see through the windows of building Number 22? I thought you said you could not see through the windows of building Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could see just a bit through the window.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But these windows were covered with a glass that is frosted. It is not clear, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The glass was -- what it was like -- I can't remember what it is called. One could not see very well through it, but one could still see.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You mean you could see light through it but you could not see -- never mind. You admit that it was not a clear glass, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could see but I do not really know what you mean when you say a clear glass.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: It was not like this glass behind your head, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, it was more like the glass of a Coca-Cola bottle, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Gestured).

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay thank you. You also stated that you were interested in weapons and hunting; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I say that? I don't believe I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I did earlier today. You said you could identify certain weapons like M-48s and automatic weapons. Did you not refer to weapons earlier today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to identify different weapons, because I had such a class at school. It was called the People's Defence, where we learned all kinds of weapons that existed in the former Yugoslavia. We used to learn about all kinds of rifles, automatic, semi-automatic, and dismantled them and everything. That is where I learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is it not true that the only weapon you were able to use in this class was an M-48? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct. We used to see the old type of a machine gun. I can't remember what it's called exactly. It's an old machine gun with the -- I think it is M-48 or M-52, the one that dates from the Second World War. We used to handle that in the class.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated earlier that Milovan Kuljanin had a gun with a scope and you said it was definitely a hunting rifle. Did you not say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a hunting weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also told this court that you know the difference between automatic and semi-automatic rifles, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I learned at school.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The only place you have had contact with these kind of weapons is at school; is that what you are telling this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on what kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The weapons that you had available to you, that the SDS provided for your friends and families in Cerici?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, he testified he knew about the guns that his friends and acquaintances had in his village before we broke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not remember hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I asked him specifically about certain people and what they had and he testified as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As to the type of guns they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your question is slightly different. You asked him something which he has not said, that the SDS provided these guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I take back the SDS part. You are familiar with the type of guns your friends and relatives had in their possession in Cerici, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think it is relevant. She wants to know he knows about these weapons. I think it is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So, Mr Draganic, would you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't know. Let me see. You are familiar with the weapons that your relatives and friends possessed in Cerici in 1992, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was familiar with the weapons from my course at school, from the course in all People's Defence, and when I saw somebody carry a rifle on their shoulder, I could identify that weapon, that rifle from the pictures that I had seen during that course in school. We did not learn only about rifles. We learned about pistols, tanks and the entire -- all the aspects of the national defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the question. The question is: you are familiar with the guns your relatives and friends have? Are you familiar with the guns your friends and relatives have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could identify the rifles that they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Earlier in your testimony you mentioned a guard named Zenga. You know Zenga is Mr Landzo and you knew Mr Landzo from high school, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I used to see him at school. That's high school.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, he is about your age, just a little bit younger, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is one year younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You knew that he hung around with a different group of people than you did at that time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just knew each other from school. This is a relatively small town and everybody knew everybody else. We knew each other because we went to the same class rooms and he was in the Forestry department and I was in the gymnasium, and both the mathematics department and the Forestry department were in the same building, the gymnasium. So I used to see him in the halls during the breaks and after our classes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You knew that he associated with many Serbian schoolboys, too, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have. I don't know. I did not pay much attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you said earlier that you knew him from the cafes or coffee shops. You knew that he hung around with a boy named Mici or Gusac, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact, that he hung around with him. He have may have; he may have not. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You knew a boy named Memco, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Memco?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Memco.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I knew him. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: While you were in school you were beaten up by a group of schoolboys, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in school.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, outside of school you were beaten up by another group of schoolboys, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not beaten up. There may have been a scuffle with one or maybe two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you told a lot of your friends at school that Mr Landzo was the one that you had the fight with, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated that he was -- well, I will take this back. Thank you. You mentioned that while you were in the Tunnel Number 9 that you were taken to an administration building and you were asked questions by an investigator, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not in Tunnel Number 9. We were taken out one by one, or maybe in pairs. I think it was one by one. So we went there, sat at the desk and they asked us our names and checked our IDs and asked other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, yesterday in your testimony you said they asked you stupid questions like: "Were you a member of the SDS? Did you have weapons?" Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. This morning you said that. All the days are running together. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me questions such as -- I don't know. They asked me about weapons, who had brought the weapons in and I did not know about that. Then who was the Commander for Cerici and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you did tell us this morning about a specific incident that you remember that happened on July 12th of 1992, did you not? I mean, besides St Peter's day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was around St Peter's day.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You talked about how an older man was beaten by Mr Landzo and other guards and how his tongue had gone back and a male nurse had come out and gotten his tongue out. Now the man you were talking about, his name was Bosko Samoukovic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about his name. He was not a doctor. He worked in a lab, blood analysis. He probably knew the basic things about how to provide assistance and first --

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr Draganic, I am sorry. I did not make myself clear. I am trying to ask you about the older gentleman that was being beaten, not the male nurse. The older gentleman, his name was Bosko Samoukovic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the name.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about a person named Miljanic. When you were first brought into the camp there was an older gentleman named Miljanic that was beaten, that died somewhere around May 27th, 1992, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that person Miljanic. I think I may have made a mistake as regards the names when I was giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much: I want to ask you: you were aware that Mr Landzo has an injury to his hand, are you not, to his right hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which hand it was, but for a while one of his hands was bandaged. I don't know if it was a plaster cast or a bandage but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You never saw any blood from this injury, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, this injury could have happened way before Celebici, could it not have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it happened in Celebici, that he sustained it in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now you testified earlier this morning that there was a Simo Jovanovic that was beaten at Celebici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You said that Mr Landzo -- from your testimony you said that Mr Landzo took him out, but from outside the only -- there were other voices but the only voice you recognised was Mr Landzo's; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: There were other voices and then you did not see who brought him back in, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the only knowledge that you have about what happened to Simo Jovanovic is the fact that Mr Landzo took him out. You do not have any personal knowledge about what happened outside the hangar, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what happened outside the hangar. I will repeat: I heard that he was beaten. You could hear the blows and you could hear the late Simo Jovanovic calling for help and moaning.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you do not know who was doing the beating outside the hangar, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You told us about a Zeljko Klimenta earlier. Now that person was friendly with the guards, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They would let him go out. He would be going out quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, the morning that you described he had gone out to have a cigarette with the guards, had he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you heard a shot outside, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then you know that one of the guards was crying and that that was an accidental shooting, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anyone cry, because I was in there, inside Number 6, and I didn't hear anyone cry.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So you really do not know what happened other than you know that there was a bullet shot and then Mr Klimenta was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I just heard the shot and then the two people who were with him outside got in and they just said: "Well, Keljo got killed".

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The guards never came into the hangar during the night, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did get in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: They came into the hangar at night-time, after dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did come in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Most of the guards were young and scared, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that they were scared, but they were young. Most of them were young.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Most of them were about your age, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You know that most of them had never served military service before this time, had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Most of the guards just followed orders, did they not? A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. We cannot hear the voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A little louder, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is all right. I will go on to the next question. You did not see Mr Landzo at Celebici before mid-June, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no sound. There is no sound. We can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the equipment might be faulty. Try and check it. The interpreters are not hearing it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Check his mike and see whether they can hear him. (Pause.) Okay. The Trial Chamber will rise for about ten, fifteen minutes, to give them sufficient time to work on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Remind him he is still a witness on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr Draganic, I just want to go back to the injury that you showed us earlier today, when you lifted your leg up here, and I wanted to ask you: that injury looked as if it had some pink fresh scratches on it. Did you recently injure it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The doctor made some examinations with a needle to verify what degree burns these are, and he examined me to see whether I had any sensation of pain in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the scrapes were caused from your examination; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated that you had put both legs up that day and that both legs were severely burnt, but you only have injury, a scar on one leg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You did not bring any medical records with you other than our examination that we have done here at the Tribunal. You have no medical records about when this injury occurred or how it occurred, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any proof of that, because when I was released to be in house arrest in Cerici, I was treated by a doctor by the name of Mikilo. He was some kind of an assistant to the doctor in the Health Care Centre. He brought some penicillin and treated the wound.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So the prosecution could have had access to these medical records. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that they could have obtained these records, because I did not go to the hospital. He came to my home, because he lives in the same village. He was married there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you did not bring any medical records with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not brought any medical records.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So this injury could have occurred in 1995, could it not have?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was a suggestion. She can put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This injury could have happened in 1995, could it not have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It could not have occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting the form it took in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can say "I suggest to you this wound was caused to you in 1995".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You could say: "I suggest to you the injury was caused in 1995." You can always make a suggestion and the witness can deny it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I suggest to you this injury could have occurred in 1995, could it not have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it could not have occurred in 1995, because there are the records of the Red Cross, the doctor from the International Red Cross. I was registered by the Red Cross on 12th August 1992, and the doctor of the Red Cross saw that I had burns on both of my legs.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: What I am saying to you is we do not have any evidence other than your testimony today that that occurred in 1992, do we?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. First of all, it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The point has been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also stated that you received medical care at Celebici seven days after this occurrence, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was. I don't know how many days, but maybe five or even seven. Maybe ten days. I don't know how many days had passed after the burning. In fact, after I was burned by him until I received medical assistance for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is because the wound was not infected until several days later, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not because of that, but because we were not allowed to leave Number 6. They started letting us go out and go there. That was for the people who had burns or other kinds of injuries. Dusko, nicknamed Sakane, had also been burned by Zenga and Spasoje. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. He is not answering my question, number one. Number two, he is testifying from absolutely no personal knowledge, unless he saw this occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What are you objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am objecting that he was testifying from no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Change your question if you do not like his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, I will. Thank you. Mr Draganic, you did not see Mr Landzo in Celebici until the middle of June when he came with a group of other guards, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when it was that I saw him. I saw him maybe in June, maybe in May. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you also stated that you didn't see him in Celebici after the end of July, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there in July. I think he left Celebici before the arrival of the Red Cross on 12th August 1992. I think so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you know for a fact that he was gone before the Red Cross arrived; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I pass the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just before I start asking any questions say this. This is a witness who is of considerable importance to the case of Mr Mucic, and I have to say that I am actually extremely tired this afternoon. I would be very grateful for your Honour's indulgence if I could cross-examine this witness tomorrow morning. As your Honours will know I am in some difficulties in representation in this case. I am effectively on my own at the moment. You will understand why I am actually quite tired at the moment. I know there is a need to keep going and keep the time up, but I am asking your Honour if that would be acceptable to you, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is Ms Residovic prepared to take over the cross-examination now? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I cross-examined a witness for a very long time this morning and in case the judges accept my colleague's suggestions, I would like to continue in the agreed order, but in case it is requested for me to start counter examination -- cross-examination, I will start that now, but I would prefer to keep to the agreed order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this puts us in a difficult position. Normally we would have -- in a normal situation we would have absolutely no objection to that. However, in this particular case because of the information that we have received from the victim witness unit which accords about the next witness, who is in a vulnerable state, a victim of sexual assault, and has been waiting around because things are behind schedule, it is very much hoped that we can get her testimony finished by the time we stop tomorrow, and we support that and we would like there to be everything done possible to make sure the next witness can be finished by the end of the day tomorrow. Therefore, for this particular case I would implore one of the defence counsel, although I understand that they are tired, to at least take advantage of this time and, in fact, we have been suggesting whether or not we should try to suggest that we go even a little over today to try to get everything done so that the next witness can be finished by the time we break for the significant period of time tomorrow, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not too satisfied with some of the reasons you have given. The question of your application from the victims witness unit is such that you have could have taken that witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Instead of this witness. You could have taken that witness to make sure that by tomorrow she will have concluded cross-examination -- or examination of that witness. At this stage at least I appreciate Mr Greaves' problem. He is alone in this matter. If they want to keep their order, because you never know what falls out from his own cross-examination, for Ms Residovic to be able to close the gap if she wants to. So it might be difficult to accommodate your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. It is certainly entirely up to the court. With respect to this particular witness, it is also the case that -- we already have, in fact, moved up the next witness. She was not supposed to be the next witness but she already was moved up, and because it was only recently that we learned how serious the problems were and, in fact, it is not her application. We did change our order around, but with respect to this witness we both did not think we could do it to be fair to this counsel, and since we had received their permission to move her up one witness but we had not asked whether or not we could start with her today and, two, this witness also has his own reasons to be back in his host country. For that reason we did not think we could switch but it is entirely your Honour's decision. I did not mean to imply something otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Some of the accused persons have greater difficulty at this stage. We will have it adjourned until tomorrow morning. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear Mrs Residovic. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I would like to thank you for the suggestions that you made. The defence did accept an exception made by the prosecutor, that is to change the order in which the witnesses are going to testify, but the defence had a special effort to make in order to prepare the cross-examination of that witness. That is why, your Honours, we would not be able to stay longer tonight after such a difficult day, and to continue cross-examining this witness. I know that at this Tribunal there are also some technical reasons that have to be taken into account, but they can never come before the right to a proper cross-examination necessary for the defence of our clients. That was why I would like to thank you, because before what I have said I have heard your opinion and I appreciate -- thank you very much for appreciating the efforts that are to be made by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour's thoughtfulness is much appreciated by me, if I may say so, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will meet again tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: --ooOoo—
